claims.text: A hybrid machine-learning model can integrate ab initio lattice-dynamics data with experimentally derived phonon and disorder descriptors.
The hybrid model will predict low lattice thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys more accurately than conventional approaches.
FeCoCrMnNi is an equiatomic or near-equiatomic crystalline high-entropy alloy with substantial intrinsic chemical disorder.
Chemical disorder in FeCoCrMnNi produces appreciable force-constant fluctuations.
Force-constant fluctuations are a dominant source of phonon scattering and attenuation in FeCoCrMnNi.
Chemical disorder in the target high-entropy alloys causes anisotropic phonon scattering.
Disorder-induced scattering governs phonon lifetimes and lattice thermal conductivity in the target alloys.
Physics-informed feature engineering will allow the model to represent nuanced disorder effects, including force-constant fluctuations.
Current first-principles and empirical prediction methods overlook important disorder-related scattering effects.
A more complete representation of disorder-related scattering mechanisms will reduce thermal-conductivity prediction error.
The hybrid model will reduce prediction error by approximately 20–30% relative to conventional methods.
The hybrid model will correctly reproduce measured trends in phonon lifetimes and linewidths in high-entropy alloys.
Combined ab initio and machine-learned-force-field methods have previously been used to predict material thermal conductivity.
The proposed approach applies under room-to-moderate-temperature conditions in which phonon conduction dominates.
The proposed approach is applicable to alloys within the compositional domain represented by its training data.
Enhanced performance is expected primarily for single-phase, near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys.
Model performance may degrade for phase-segregated alloys or for disorder and compositions outside the training domain.
Failure to obtain roughly a 20–30% error reduction over conventional methods would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to reproduce measured disorder-related phonon scattering and thermal-conductivity behavior would falsify the hypothesis.
